title: How To Fix A Big Classroom Management Mistake istake/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin addresses the inevitable moment when a teacher mistakenly enforces a consequence on the wrong student, risking a serious loss of rapport and trust. He lays out an eight-step protocol for correcting the error: being proactive about the possibility of mistakes, modeling how students should raise concerns, handling the correction immediately, hearing the student privately, determining the truth of the claim, consulting a witness only if necessary, apologizing publicly and directly, and — if the student turns out to be mistaken — moving on without further discussion. He closes by reassuring teachers that empowering students to point out errors builds trust and confidence rather than encouraging dishonesty, since students appreciate having a voice and knowing they won't be held accountable for something they didn't do.
points: Teachers should proactively tell students, as part of teaching the classroom management plan, that mistakes can happen and should be reported immediately.
Mistaken consequences must be corrected right away, not after the lesson, since delay leaves a wrongly-punished student stewing in resentment.
The correction process involves privately hearing the student's account, judging its credibility, and — rarely — confirming with a witness.
A public apology should be direct and succinct, modeling accountability for the whole class to see.
Empowering students to speak up about mistakes builds loyalty and trust, and teaches them to advocate for themselves and others.
quotes: But when you send a student to time-out who didn’t deserve it, you risk losing the rapport, influence, and trust you’ve worked so ardently to achieve. It can disappear in a flash of anger, betrayal, and resentment.
It’s important to correct your mistake right away. If you wait until your lesson is over, it’s too late.
In most circumstances, you’ll know straight away if you got it wrong. The student’s story, along with his body language and tone of voice, will ring true.
Apologize to the student in front of the class. Be direct and succinct. “Class, I owe Joseph an apology. I thought he broke a rule, but it was a misunderstanding—and my fault. So, Joseph, I’m sorry.

Contrary to causing them to be untruthful or argumentative, teaching your students how to square their shoulders and candidly point out injustice engenders loyalty and trust and the confidence to speak up not only for themselves… But for those in society who don’t have a voice.
